That is the exact reason why people can still win at a casino. The house always wins not by always beating the individual - that would stop people from returning - but instead by taking a cut of the total *turnover* from the game. They take this cut by using the house edge - rules that make certain that if someone bets on all the options, they will not break even, but lose a little (usually about 5%).     Roulette is the simplest example:   Person A comes in and bets on black, and wins $10. He then leaves the casino, up $10. The house is now down $10.   Person B then comes in and bets on black, but loses his $10. But for the house, all this does is bring the loss back down to $0. Every now and then, however, the ball lands on the green "0" number, and both Red and Black bets lose. This only has a small chance of happening (1 in 37), so overtime the house collects approximately 5% of the total money that comes through the table.       The important part, however, is that nothing past what Patron A did has any effect on what he won - which is still $10. So whilst the casino is making money (the house always wins), there are still people who have also won money on their trip to the casino.      And that is the ultimate draw of the casino - to try your luck at being Patron A, the one who won.

I think it's misleading to say that the house is always 'winning'. It is making money, but that is not the same thing as winning; just because the house made money does not mean that everyone who went to the casino on that day lost. I really quite like the prequel, but it does have a few aspects that were disappointing compared to the remake, which came out just prior to its release. * First of all, the story is really silly. The remake had an amazing story, even more so than the first game, because of the addition of a specific character, which was an incredibly creepy subplot. Everything that happens in the game is pretty plausible if you accept the parameters of the story. In the prequel, however, we are given a singing leech man in a white dress with anime hair, who constantly goes on bizarre monologues. On top of that, the exchanges between the two main villains are possibly the most cringeworthy in the series so far, and the exposition is very ham fisted. Instead of experiencing the story through notes and events that happen to the player, we are given bizarre and jarring flashbacks and perspective changes. It felt more like a soap opera than a horror game or movie. * Secondly, the pacing of the game. The prequel starts off really well - the train is fantastic, and the Training Facility is pretty damn good (if a little slow near the end), but then the game takes a bizarre turn pacing wise. We are moved rapidly from location to location, including a strange expedition into a specific lab from the sequel, which, whilst it was a pretty cool glimpse at what a remake would be like, was quite obviously just there for fanservice, and created way more questions than it answered. The Factory also gave birth to the infamous, immersion breaking magic elevator, which confused the hell out of people (with good reason). The final areas of the game, which are supposed to be the most engaging, ended up being a pretty linear series of rooms that just lead to the last boss. * Thirdly, the new gameplay mechanics. They were actually pretty cool ideas - no more item box backtracking, and some extra gameplay in the form of character switching. Unfortunately, the item design that was supposed to combat backtracking was completely pointless, as it just resulted in designated 'item rooms' anyway, which were usually right next to a typewriter, just as the original item boxes were. It actually caused more problems, because the game designers no longer had to worry too much about players running out of inventory space, as they could just drop items. So we have lots of items in the game that take up two slots, and end up being ferried around from location to location (hookshot, I'm looking at you). Combine that with the constant item juggling between characters, and the ability to make bad decisions when splitting up that can adversely effect your experience (do NOT send one character up stairs in the Lab), and the result is a much more frustrating and less immersive experience. Look, the prequel is still a great game. I prefer it to other entries in the series as a survival horror game, but compared to the beautiful pacing and atmosphere of the remake and the sequel, it simply doesn't hold up as well. *it may not be that specific lab, but the fanservice intent is clear.

Voice acting is a brutal business, so for anyone with any idea of making it a career, unions are a must. Unfortunately there is always a big pool of new and naive talent to take advantage of by these localization companies.

For a voice actor, royalties *is* fair pay. The reason for this is the very same as what is happening to a certain actress now; VAs are easily replaced. They have zero job security, because unlike a regular actor whose face is a key aspect of their character's identity, VAs can get thrown out the second they ask for any kind of increase in pay. Of course, the natural result of this is that studios can go the other way - completely underpay VAs, because they need all the work they can get. View the work history of a standard TV actor and you'll see a handful of different shows, but look at the history for the same level VA, and you'll often see hundreds of different projects, shows and games. The VA is earning a sliver of what an actor would be. *"VAs should get properly paid for the work up front and that should be the end of it."* is completely true - but the reality is that they don't. Ironically, the only voice actors who get paid adequately are the ones who are already big name actors - and they also often turn out to be terrible VAs.       I personally hate the state of most industry unions, but VA is one of the few that really does need support, because even with it they still get shit on.
